title: The borrowed colt (Mark 11:1–11)
hookLine: the Lord has need of it: the entry into Jerusalem on an unridden colt
carry: the lord has need of it
tomorrow: the fig tree and the temple

lines: THE LORD HATH NEED OF HIM.
cards: Two strangers walk up to a car in a driveway, unlock it, and start to drive off. The owner runs out: what are you doing? They say one sentence, and the owner lets them go.

That's roughly what happens here. Jesus and his friends reach the Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem. He sends two of them into the village ahead: you'll find a colt tied up that no one has ever ridden.
Untie it and bring it. If anyone asks why, in the King James Bible, "say ye that the Lord hath need of him; and straightway he will send him hither." It's there, tied by a door in the street.
People standing by ask: what are you doing, untying that colt? They give the answer, and the people let them go.

teach.h: WHO OWNED IT? MARK IS SILENT.
teach.b: Who owned the colt? Mark doesn't say. A friend, maybe, or someone told ahead; the text is silent.
What it keeps is the loan: someone let go of something valuable, on a single sentence, because the Lord had need of it. They throw their garments on the colt, and Jesus sits on it.

teach.h: GARMENTS AND BRANCHES ON THE ROAD.
teach.b: People spread their garments on the road, and others, in the King James words, cut down branches off the trees. Mark doesn't say palms; those come from John's Gospel, and give Palm Sunday its name.
The crowd shouts: "Hosanna; Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord."
Hosanna comes from Hebrew and means something like save, please. In the crowd's mouth, it rings out like praise. The words echo Psalm 118.
Why a colt, not a warhorse? Matthew and John quote the prophet Zechariah: your king comes to you, lowly, riding on a donkey. Mark doesn't quote it, but some readers hear it anyway.
Then Mark's ending. After all the shouting, he goes into the temple, looks around at everything, and since it's late, walks back out to Bethany with the twelve. No speech.

teach.h: BLESSED IS HE THAT COMETH IN THE NAME OF THE LORD.
teach.b: Christians remember this day as Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week, and in churches that keep it, people carry palms or branches and sing hosanna.

how: Christians remember this entry on Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week; in churches that keep the day, people carry palm branches in procession and sing hosanna, and the palms are sometimes kept and later burned for the next year's Ash Wednesday.

games.q: you're standing by a doorway when two strangers untie a young colt. you ask what they're doing. they say: the Lord hath need of him. what do you do?
o: stop them until the owner comes.
games.why: the bystanders let them go. one sentence, and a valuable animal is lent freely.

practice: Picture the things you keep tied up by your own front door: your car, your tools, your time on Saturday, your spare room. Who could use one of them?
Picture untying it and letting it go, no fuss, no conditions, trusting it to come back, and be gentle with whatever makes you hesitate; if you pray, you can offer what you have to God's use.

wordCard.voice: Hosanna, a Hebrew cry meaning save, please, that the crowd shouted as praise. A borrowed colt, lent on one sentence, carried Jesus into Jerusalem.
